decks.title: Statistics: Part 1, collecting data, frequency tables, bar graphs and stacked bar graphs
goals: Tell primary data from secondary data and collect data in a table
Make frequency tables with tally marks, and grouped frequency tables with class intervals
Read and interpret stacked bar graphs, including the totals and the parts

slides.heading: Counting and picturing data
slides.body_md: **Statistics** is the study of collecting, organising and picturing **data** so that we can answer questions. A bar graph makes the favourite drinks of $30$ students easy to see.

visual.alt: Bar graph of the favourite drink of 30 students: tea 8, milk 11, juice 6 and lassi 5. The tallest bar is milk.
visual.caption: A bar graph: each bar stands for one drink and its height is the number of students.

slides.narration: Which drink do students like best? To find out, we ask, we count, and we draw. Statistics is the study of collecting data, organising it in tables, and showing it in pictures. In this part we make tables with tally marks, group data into classes, and read bar graphs and stacked bar graphs.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Make a **frequency table** with tally marks

visual.alt: Flow of Part 1: collecting data, tally marks and frequency tables, grouped frequency tables, bar graphs and stacked bar graphs.
visual.caption: Part 1 road map.

slides.narration: First we see where data comes from. Then we count with tally marks and build frequency tables, and we group large data into classes. At the end we read bar graphs, and stacked bar graphs, where each bar is cut into parts.

slides.heading: Primary and secondary data
slides.body_md: Facts and figures collected for a purpose are called **data**. Before using data, ask: **who collected it, and why?**

rows: Collected by you or your team, for your own purpose, by a survey, an interview, a measurement or an experiment
A class in Indore counts the shoe sizes of its own students
Collected earlier by someone else and taken from a source such as a report, a newspaper or a website
A student uses the yearly rainfall figures of a city from a weather department report

visual.alt: Table of two kinds of data. Primary data is collected by you or your team for your own purpose, for example a class counting the shoe sizes of its own students. Secondary data was collected earlier by someone else and is taken from a source such as a report, a newspaper or a website, for example the yearly rainfall figures from a weather department report.
visual.caption: You collect primary data yourself; someone else collected secondary data.

slides.narration: Data are facts and numbers collected for a purpose. If you collect them yourself, by asking, measuring or counting, they are primary data. If someone else collected them earlier and you take them from a report, a newspaper or a website, they are secondary data. Ask who collected the data, and why.

slides.heading: Tally marks
slides.body_md: To count a long list, go through it once and make **one stroke for each value**. Draw the fifth stroke **across** the four. The number of strokes is the **frequency**.

visual.alt: Table of tally marks: one stroke for each value, and every fifth stroke is drawn across the four before it. One is a single stroke, two is two strokes, four is four strokes, five is four strokes crossed by a slash, seven is five and two strokes, and twelve is two crossed groups of five and two strokes.
visual.caption: Tally marks come in groups of five, so a long tally is easy to count.

slides.narration: A tally is a quick way to count. For each value in the list, draw one stroke. When you reach five, draw the fifth stroke across the first four. Groups of five are easy to count later. The total number of strokes for a value is called its frequency.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: shoe sizes
slides.body_md: The shoe sizes of $30$ students are: 7, 6, 8, 7, 5, 6, 7, 9, 7, 8, 6, 7, 8, 5, 7, 6, 9, 7, 8, 6, 7, 8, 6, 7, 9, 5, 7, 8, 6, 7. Make a frequency table.
bullets: **Tally —** go through the list once, one stroke per size

visual.alt: Frequency table of the shoe sizes of 30 students: size 5 has 3 students, size 6 has 7, size 7 has 11, size 8 has 6 and size 9 has 3. The frequencies add up to 30.
visual.caption: The sum of the frequencies is the number of observations.

slides.narration: We go through the thirty sizes once, and make a stroke for each. Size five has three strokes, size six has seven, size seven has eleven, size eight has six, and size nine has three. As a check, the frequencies add up to thirty, which is the number of students. The most common size is seven.

slides.heading: Grouping data into classes
slides.body_md: When there are many different values, we **group** them into **class intervals**. Every value goes into exactly one class: the **lower limit is included**, the upper limit goes to the next class.

rows: A group of values, from a lower limit to an upper limit
The lower limit belongs to the class, the upper limit belongs to the next class
The mid-point of the class: (lower + upper) ÷ 2
The number of observations in the class
$11$ students (from the table of homework times)

visual.alt: Table of terms for grouped data. A class interval such as 30 to 45 has a lower limit 30 which is included and an upper limit 45 which belongs to the next class. Its class width is 45 minus 30, which is 15, its class mark is the mid-point 37.5, and its frequency is the number of observations in it, 11 in the homework data.
visual.caption: In grouped data every value goes into exactly one class.

slides.narration: If the values are many and spread out, a table with one row per value is too long. So we group them into classes, such as thirty to forty-five. The lower limit belongs to the class, and the upper limit belongs to the next class. The class width is the upper limit minus the lower limit, and the class mark is the middle of the class.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: homework times
bullets: **Boundary —** the value $30$ goes in $30$–$45$, not in $15$–$30$

visual.alt: Grouped frequency table of the homework times of 40 students in classes of width 15 minutes: 0 to 15 has 2 students, 15 to 30 has 6, 30 to 45 has 11, 45 to 60 has 12, 60 to 75 has 7 and 75 to 90 has 2. The class marks are 7.5, 22.5, 37.5, 52.5, 67.5 and 82.5.
visual.caption: Grouped frequency table of the homework times; the classes do not overlap.

slides.narration: The smallest value is eight and the largest is eighty-five, so classes of width fifteen from zero to ninety are enough. We tally each value in its class. A value such as thirty goes in the class thirty to forty-five, because the lower limit is included. The frequencies are two, six, eleven, twelve, seven and two, and they add up to forty.

slides.heading: Quick check: the boundary
slides.body_md: In the grouped table of homework times, the classes are zero to fifteen, fifteen to thirty, thirty to forty-five, and so on. In which class does a student who worked exactly thirty minutes go?

visual.alt: Grouped frequency table of the homework times of 40 students in classes of width 15 minutes: 0 to 15 has 2 students, 15 to 30 has 6, 30 to 45 has 11, 45 to 60 has 12, 60 to 75 has 7 and 75 to 90 has 2. The class marks are 7.5, 22.5, 37.5, 52.5, 67.5 and 82.5.
visual.caption: Grouped frequency table of the homework times; the classes do not overlap.

slides.narration: Remember which limit is included.

slides.heading: Bar graphs
slides.body_md: A **bar graph** shows the frequency of each category as the **height** of a bar. The bars have the **same width** and **gaps** between them, and the scale starts at $0$.

visual.alt: Bar graph of the shoe sizes of 30 students: size 5 has 3 students, size 6 has 7, size 7 has 11, size 8 has 6 and size 9 has 3. The tallest bar is size 7.
visual.caption: Bar graph of the frequency table of shoe sizes: the height of a bar is the frequency.

slides.narration: A bar graph turns a frequency table into a picture. Each bar stands for one value, and its height shows the frequency. The bars have equal width, there are gaps between them, and the scale on the side starts at zero. The tallest bar, here for size seven, shows the most common value at a glance.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: reading a bar graph
slides.body_md: Use the bar graph of shoe sizes to answer questions about the $30$ students.

rows: Which size is the most common?
How many students wear size $8$ or more?
How many wear a size smaller than $7$?

visual.alt: Table of readings from the bar graph of shoe sizes: the tallest bar is size 7 with 11 students; sizes 8 or more have 6 plus 3, which is 9 students; sizes smaller than 7 have 3 plus 7, which is 10 students; the total is 30 students.
visual.caption: Read a bar graph by looking at the height of each bar against the scale.

slides.narration: To read a bar graph, look at the height of each bar against the scale. The tallest bar is size seven, with eleven students. For sizes eight or more, add six and three to get nine students. For sizes smaller than seven, add three and seven to get ten. All the bars together give thirty.

slides.heading: Quick check: favourite drinks
slides.body_md: In the bar graph of favourite drinks, tea has eight students and lassi has five. How many students chose tea or lassi?

visual.alt: Bar graph of the favourite drink of 30 students: tea 8, milk 11, juice 6 and lassi 5. The tallest bar is milk.
visual.caption: A bar graph: each bar stands for one drink and its height is the number of students.

slides.narration: Add the two bars.

slides.heading: Stacked bar graphs
slides.body_md: In a **stacked bar graph** each bar is cut into **parts** that are piled up. The **whole bar** shows the **total**, and each part shows one kind. The number above the bar is the total.

visual.alt: Stacked bar graph of the items sold in a school canteen from Monday to Friday. Each bar has three parts, from the bottom: samosas, sandwiches and juices. On Monday 30 samosas, 20 sandwiches and 15 juices make 65 items; Tuesday 25, 30 and 20 make 75; Wednesday 40, 25 and 10 make 75; Thursday 35, 35 and 25 make 95; Friday 45, 30 and 20 make 95.
visual.caption: Stacked bars: from the bottom the parts are samosas (shaded), sandwiches (coloured) and juices (outlined); the number above a bar is the total.

slides.narration: A stacked bar graph shows two things at once. The whole bar is the total for the day, and each coloured part is one kind of item. Here, a school canteen sold samosas, sandwiches and juices from Monday to Friday. The number on each part is its amount, and the number above the bar is the total.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: reading stacked bars
slides.body_md: Answer questions about the canteen sales from the stacked bar graph.

rows: The top part of the Wednesday bar
The middle part of the Friday bar
Items sold in the whole week

visual.alt: Table of readings from the stacked bar graph: Thursday total 35 plus 35 plus 25 is 95; Wednesday juices are 10; Friday sandwiches are 30; samosas in the week are 30 plus 25 plus 40 plus 35 plus 45, which is 175; all items in the week are 65 plus 75 plus 75 plus 95 plus 95, which is 405.
visual.caption: The whole bar gives the total; each part gives one kind.

slides.narration: The whole bar for Thursday is the sum of its three parts, thirty-five, thirty-five and twenty-five, which is ninety-five. To get the samosas for the week, add the bottom parts of all five bars, which gives one hundred seventy-five. All items together are four hundred five, and the same total comes from adding the three weekly totals for samosas, sandwiches and juices.

slides.heading: Choosing the right graph
slides.body_md: The question decides the picture. A stacked bar graph is best when we want **both the total and the parts**.

rows: The amounts of separate categories, such as favourite drinks
How each total is split into parts, such as items sold each day
The frequencies of grouped data, such as minutes or units
The shape of a distribution, or two distributions together

visual.alt: Table of which graph to use: a bar graph for amounts of separate categories, a stacked bar graph for how each total is split into parts, a histogram for the frequencies of grouped data, and a frequency polygon for the shape of a distribution or for comparing two.
visual.caption: Choose the graph that matches the question.

slides.narration: Which graph should we draw? For separate categories, a bar graph. To show how each total splits into parts, a stacked bar graph. For grouped numbers like minutes or units, a histogram, which we meet in the next part. To show the shape of a distribution, a frequency polygon.

slides.heading: Quick check: stacked bars
slides.body_md: On Thursday the canteen sold thirty-five samosas and twenty-five juices. How many more samosas than juices were sold?

visual.alt: Stacked bar graph of the items sold in a school canteen from Monday to Friday. Each bar has three parts, from the bottom: samosas, sandwiches and juices. On Monday 30 samosas, 20 sandwiches and 15 juices make 65 items; Tuesday 25, 30 and 20 make 75; Wednesday 40, 25 and 10 make 75; Thursday 35, 35 and 25 make 95; Friday 45, 30 and 20 make 95.
visual.caption: Stacked bars: from the bottom the parts are samosas (shaded), sandwiches (coloured) and juices (outlined); the number above a bar is the total.

slides.narration: Subtract the juice part from the samosa part.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: **Primary** data you collect yourself; **secondary** data come from a source
A **frequency table** counts values with tally marks; the frequencies add up to the number of observations
A **class** has a lower limit (included), an upper limit, a **width** and a **class mark** (the mid-point)
A **bar graph** has equal bars with gaps; a **stacked bar** has parts that add up to the total

visual.alt: Summary flow of Part 1: primary or secondary data, tally marks and frequency, classes with their width and mark, and bar graphs including stacked bar graphs.
visual.caption: Four steps of Part 1.

slides.narration: To sum up. Primary data are collected by you, and secondary data come from a source. We count with tally marks, and the frequencies add up to the number of observations. For grouped data, each class has a lower limit, a width and a class mark. A bar graph shows amounts, and a stacked bar graph shows both the total and the parts.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Frequency tables (2–3 marks):** use tally marks, then check that the frequencies add up to the total
**Reading graphs:** read the scale first and give the unit
**Mistake:** putting a value equal to an upper limit into that class
**Mistake:** reading a stacked part as the total
slides.narration: For a frequency table, make the tally, write the frequencies, and check that they add up to the total number. When reading a graph, read the scale first and give the unit in your answer. Two common slips are putting a value equal to the upper limit into that class, and reading one part of a stacked bar as the whole total.

decks.title: Statistics: Part 2, weighted average, histograms and frequency polygons
goals: Compute a weighted average and tell it from the simple mean
Use the weighted average for grades, prices and cost-of-living figures
Draw and read histograms with equal and unequal class widths
Draw a frequency polygon from a frequency table

slides.heading: Fair averages and pictures of grouped data
slides.body_md: Some values matter **more** than others, so we give them a **weight**. And grouped data are drawn as a **histogram**, a bar graph with no gaps.

visual.alt: Histogram of the electricity used by 50 households in classes of width 50 units. The heights are 4, 9, 15, 12, 6 and 4 for the classes 100 to 150, 150 to 200, 200 to 250, 250 to 300, 300 to 350 and 350 to 400.
visual.caption: Histogram of the units used by 50 households: classes of width $50$ units.

slides.narration: Is it fair to give a final exam and a class test the same importance? Often not. A weighted average lets each value count according to its weight. In this part we also draw histograms and frequency polygons, the pictures that show how grouped numbers are spread out.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do

visual.alt: Flow of Part 2: the weighted mean, histograms with equal class widths, histograms with unequal class widths and frequency density, and frequency polygons.
visual.caption: Part 2 road map.

slides.narration: We begin with the weighted average, and use it for exam grades, for the price of a mixture, and for the change in the cost of living. Then we draw histograms, first with equal classes and then with unequal classes using frequency density. Last, we join class marks to make a frequency polygon.

slides.heading: The weighted mean
slides.body_md: If the values $x_1, x_2, \ldots$ have **weights** $w_1, w_2, \ldots$, the **weighted mean** is $\dfrac{x_1 w_1 + x_2 w_2 + \cdots}{w_1 + w_2 + \cdots}$.

visual.alt: Table of a weighted mean: class tests with mark 60 and weight 2 give 120, the project with mark 70 and weight 3 gives 210, and the final exam with mark 90 and weight 5 gives 450. The total weight is 10 and the total of mark times weight is 780, so the weighted mean is 78.
visual.caption: Weighted mean = total of (value × weight) ÷ total of the weights.

slides.narration: In a weighted mean, each value is multiplied by its weight. Add all these products, and divide by the total of the weights. In the table, class tests, the project and the final exam have weights two, three and five. The total of the products is seven hundred eighty, and the total weight is ten, so the weighted mean is seventy-eight.

slides.heading: Simple mean or weighted mean?
slides.body_md: The **simple mean** gives every value the same importance. The **weighted mean** is different whenever the weights are different, and the same when they are all equal.

rows: Each value counts according to its weight
Always the same as the weighted mean when all weights are equal
Different when the weights are different

visual.alt: Table comparing the simple mean and the weighted mean. For the scores 72, 85 and 64 with weights 2, 3 and 5, the simple mean is 221 over 3, about 73.67, and the weighted mean is 719 over 10, which is 71.9. The two are the same when all the weights are equal.
visual.caption: The weighted mean follows the value with the largest weight.

slides.narration: The simple mean treats every value alike. Take the scores seventy-two, eighty-five and sixty-four. Their simple mean is about seventy-three point six seven. But if the weights are two, three and five, the weighted mean is seventy-one point nine, lower, because the lowest score has the largest weight. If all weights are equal, the two means agree.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a final grade
slides.body_md: A student has scores $72$ in class tests, $85$ in the project and $64$ in the final exam, with weights $2$, $3$ and $5$. Find the weighted mean.

visual.alt: Table: scores 72, 85 and 64 with weights 2, 3 and 5 give 144, 255 and 320. The total is 719 and the total weight is 10, so the weighted mean is 71.9, lower than the simple mean 73.67 because the lowest score has the largest weight.
visual.caption: The final exam has the largest weight and the lowest score, so it pulls the mean down.

slides.narration: Multiply each score by its weight. That gives one hundred forty-four, two hundred fifty-five and three hundred twenty. Their total is seven hundred nineteen. The weights add up to ten. So the weighted mean is seventy-one point nine. It is lower than the simple mean because the final exam, with the largest weight, had the lowest score.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a mixture of rice
slides.body_md: A trader in Karnal mixes $30$ kg of rice at $\text{Rs } 42$ per kg, $20$ kg at $\text{Rs } 55$ per kg and $50$ kg at $\text{Rs } 60$ per kg. Find the average price of the mixture per kg.

visual.alt: Table: a trader mixes 30 kilograms of rice at 42 rupees per kilogram, 20 kilograms at 55 and 50 kilograms at 60. The costs are 1260, 1100 and 3000 rupees, 5360 rupees for 100 kilograms, so the average price is 53.6 rupees per kilogram.
visual.caption: The quantities are the weights.

slides.narration: The quantities are the weights. The three costs are one thousand two hundred sixty, one thousand one hundred, and three thousand rupees. Together that is five thousand three hundred sixty rupees for one hundred kilograms. So the average price is fifty-three point six rupees per kilogram. The simple mean of the three prices would be only about fifty-two point three three.

slides.heading: Quick check: a mixture of dal
slides.body_md: A shopkeeper mixes twenty kilograms of dal at ninety rupees per kilogram with thirty kilograms at eighty rupees per kilogram. What is the average price per kilogram?

visual.alt: Table: a trader mixes 30 kilograms of rice at 42 rupees per kilogram, 20 kilograms at 55 and 50 kilograms at 60. The costs are 1260, 1100 and 3000 rupees, 5360 rupees for 100 kilograms, so the average price is 53.6 rupees per kilogram.
visual.caption: The quantities are the weights.

slides.narration: The quantities are the weights.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a cost-of-living basket
slides.body_md: In a family budget, food has weight $5$ and its price rose $8\%$, housing has weight $3$ and rose $4\%$, and transport has weight $2$ and rose $10\%$. Find the overall rise.

visual.alt: Table: a family budget has food with weight 5 and a price rise of 8 percent, housing with weight 3 and a rise of 4 percent, and transport with weight 2 and a rise of 10 percent. The products are 40, 12 and 20, which add up to 72. Divided by the total weight 10, the weighted rise is 7.2 percent, a little less than the simple mean 7.33 percent.
visual.caption: A cost-of-living figure weights each item by its share of the budget.

slides.narration: A cost of living figure weights each item by its share of the budget. Food has weight five and rose eight percent, so the product is forty. Housing gives twelve and transport gives twenty. The total is seventy-two, and the weights add up to ten. So prices rose by seven point two percent overall.

slides.heading: Histograms
slides.body_md: For grouped data we draw a **histogram**: a bar for each class, **no gaps**, the width of a bar is the **class width** and, for equal widths, the **height** is the **frequency**.

visual.alt: Histogram of the homework time of 40 students in classes of width 15 minutes. The bars have heights 2, 6, 11, 12, 7 and 2 for the classes 0 to 15, 15 to 30, 30 to 45, 45 to 60, 60 to 75 and 75 to 90. The bars touch each other.
visual.caption: Histogram of the homework times: equal class widths, so the height of a bar shows the frequency.

slides.narration: A histogram is the picture of a grouped frequency table. Each class gets a bar, and the bars touch each other, because the classes follow each other without a break. When all classes have the same width, the height of a bar shows the frequency. Here the tallest bar is for forty-five to sixty minutes of homework.

slides.heading: Histogram or bar graph?
slides.body_md: Both use bars, but they show **different kinds of data**.

rows: No: the classes follow each other
Fixed, in the order of the classes

visual.alt: Table comparing a bar graph and a histogram. A bar graph shows separate categories, has gaps between the bars, the bars can be put in any order, and the width of a bar has no meaning. A histogram shows grouped numbers, has no gaps, the bars are in the order of the classes, and the width of a bar is the class width.
visual.caption: A histogram is a bar graph for classes of numbers.

slides.narration: A bar graph shows separate categories, so it has gaps, and its bars can be moved around. A histogram shows classes of numbers, so there are no gaps, and the bars stay in the order of the classes. In a histogram, the width of a bar is the class width.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: drawing a histogram
slides.body_md: The units of electricity used by $50$ households are grouped in classes of width $50$. Draw the histogram.
bullets: **Scale —** $100$ to $400$ units on the axis, frequency from $0$ to $16$

visual.alt: Histogram of the electricity used by 50 households in classes of width 50 units. The heights are 4, 9, 15, 12, 6 and 4 for the classes 100 to 150, 150 to 200, 200 to 250, 250 to 300, 300 to 350 and 350 to 400.
visual.caption: Histogram of the units used by 50 households: classes of width $50$ units.

slides.narration: Mark the units from one hundred to four hundred on the bottom axis, and the number of households up the side. The classes have equal width, so the heights are the frequencies, four, nine, fifteen, twelve, six and four. Draw the bars next to each other. The tallest bar is for two hundred to two hundred fifty units.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading a histogram
slides.body_md: In the histogram of electricity use, how many households used two hundred units or more?

visual.alt: Histogram of the electricity used by 50 households in classes of width 50 units. The heights are 4, 9, 15, 12, 6 and 4 for the classes 100 to 150, 150 to 200, 200 to 250, 250 to 300, 300 to 350 and 350 to 400.
visual.caption: Histogram of the units used by 50 households: classes of width $50$ units.

slides.narration: Add the bars from two hundred onwards.

slides.heading: Unequal class widths
slides.body_md: When class widths differ, a bar's height cannot be the frequency. Use the **frequency density** $= \dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$. Then the **area** of a bar is the frequency.

visual.alt: Histogram of the ages of 100 visitors of a science museum with unequal class widths. The height of each bar is the frequency per year of age: 1.8 for 10 to 20, 3 for 20 to 30, 2.4 for 30 to 40, 1 for 40 to 60 and 0.2 for 60 to 100. The areas of the bars are the frequencies 18, 30, 24, 20 and 8.
visual.caption: Unequal class widths: the height is the frequency density, so the area of a bar is the frequency.

slides.narration: Sometimes the classes have different widths. If we drew the frequency as the height, a wide class would look too important. So we use frequency density, which is frequency divided by class width. Then the area of each bar is the frequency, and the picture is fair. Here the classes for ages forty to sixty and sixty to one hundred are wider.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: frequency density
slides.body_md: The ages of $100$ visitors of a museum are grouped in unequal classes. Find the height of each bar.

visual.alt: Table of the ages of 100 visitors of a science museum with unequal class widths. The classes 10 to 20, 20 to 30 and 30 to 40 have width 10 and frequencies 18, 30 and 24, so the densities are 1.8, 3 and 2.4. The class 40 to 60 has width 20 and frequency 20, so the density is 1. The class 60 to 100 has width 40 and frequency 8, so the density is 0.2.
visual.caption: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.

slides.narration: For each class, divide the frequency by the class width. For ten to twenty, eighteen divided by ten is one point eight. For forty to sixty, twenty divided by twenty is one. For sixty to one hundred, eight divided by forty is point two. As a check, the area of each bar, height times width, gives back the frequency.

slides.heading: Frequency polygons
slides.body_md: A **frequency polygon** joins the points (**class mark**, **frequency**). Add an **empty class** with frequency $0$ at each end, so that the polygon starts and ends on the axis.

visual.alt: Frequency polygon of the electricity used by 50 households: the points are 75 with 0 households, 125 with 4, 175 with 9, 225 with 15, 275 with 12, 325 with 6, 375 with 4 and 425 with 0, joined by straight lines.
visual.caption: Frequency polygon: class marks against frequencies, with an empty class at each end.

slides.narration: A frequency polygon is a second way to picture grouped data. Find the class mark of each class, which is its middle value, and plot the frequency above it. Join the points with straight lines. At both ends, add an empty class with frequency zero, so that the polygon begins and ends on the axis.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: points of the polygon
slides.body_md: Find the points of the frequency polygon for the electricity data, with the classes $50$–$100$ and $400$–$450$ added.

visual.alt: Table of the points of the frequency polygon: the class mark 75 with frequency 0 for an extra empty class, then 125 with 4, 175 with 9, 225 with 15, 275 with 12, 325 with 6 and 375 with 4, and the class mark 425 with frequency 0 for a second extra empty class.
visual.caption: Add an empty class at each end so that the polygon starts and ends on the axis.

slides.narration: The class mark of a class is the average of its two limits. For one hundred to one hundred fifty it is one hundred twenty-five. We add two empty classes, fifty to one hundred and four hundred to four hundred fifty, with class marks seventy-five and four hundred twenty-five and frequency zero. Plot the eight points and join them in order.

slides.heading: A polygon over a histogram
slides.body_md: The polygon passes through the **mid-points of the tops** of the bars. Both pictures show the same data, the histogram by areas of bars, the polygon by a line.

visual.alt: The histogram of the electricity used by 50 households with its frequency polygon drawn over it. The polygon joins the mid-points of the tops of the bars, 125, 175, 225, 275, 325 and 375, and is closed on the axis at the class marks 75 and 425 of two extra classes with frequency 0.
visual.caption: The frequency polygon joins the mid-points of the tops of the bars; it starts and ends on the axis at the mid-points of the empty classes $50$ to $100$ and $400$ to $450$.

slides.narration: Here the polygon is drawn over the histogram. It goes through the middle of the top of every bar. At the left and the right it comes down to the axis, at the class marks of the two empty classes. The polygon is handy when we want to draw two distributions on the same axes and compare them.

slides.heading: Quick check: the empty classes
slides.body_md: For the classes one hundred to one hundred fifty up to three hundred fifty to four hundred, a frequency polygon is closed with two empty classes. At which class marks does it touch the axis?

visual.alt: Frequency polygon of the electricity used by 50 households: the points are 75 with 0 households, 125 with 4, 175 with 9, 225 with 15, 275 with 12, 325 with 6, 375 with 4 and 425 with 0, joined by straight lines.
visual.caption: Frequency polygon: class marks against frequencies, with an empty class at each end.

slides.narration: Use the middle of each empty class.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: **Weighted mean** $= \dfrac{\sum xw}{\sum w}$; equal weights give the simple mean
**Histogram:** bars touch; for equal widths the height is the frequency
**Unequal widths:** height $=$ frequency density $= \dfrac{f}{\text{width}}$, so area $=$ frequency
**Frequency polygon:** points (class mark, frequency), with an empty class at each end

nodes.label: Weighted mean: sum of value x weight / sum of weights

sections.heading: 1. Collecting and organising data
sections.body_md: **Data** are facts and figures collected for a purpose. **Primary data** are collected by you; **secondary data** were collected earlier by someone else and are taken from a source. A **frequency table** counts each value with **tally marks** (groups of five, the fifth stroke across the four); the **frequencies** add up to the number of observations.

key_terms.definition_md: Data collected by the investigator for the purpose in hand.
Data collected earlier by someone else and taken from a source.
The number of times a value, or the number of observations in a class, occurs.

sections.heading: 2. Grouped frequency tables
sections.body_md: When there are many values we group them into **class intervals**. The **lower limit** belongs to the class and the **upper limit** to the next class. **Class width** = upper limit $-$ lower limit; **class mark** = $\dfrac{\text{lower} + \text{upper}}{2}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A group of values such as 30–45.
Upper limit minus lower limit of the class.

rows: A group of values, from a lower limit to an upper limit
The lower limit belongs to the class, the upper limit belongs to the next class
The mid-point of the class: (lower + upper) ÷ 2
The number of observations in the class

sections.heading: 3. Weighted average
sections.body_md: If the values $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ have weights $w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_n$, the **weighted mean** is $\dfrac{x_1w_1 + x_2w_2 + \cdots + x_nw_n}{w_1 + w_2 + \cdots + w_n}$. It differs from the **simple mean** unless the weights are equal. Uses: a **weighted exam score**, the **average price per kg** of a mixture (quantities are the weights) and a **cost-of-living** figure (shares of the budget are the weights).

key_terms.definition_md: A number that says how much a value counts.
The total of value times weight, divided by the total of the weights.

visual.alt: Table of a weighted mean: class tests with mark 60 and weight 2 give 120, the project with mark 70 and weight 3 gives 210, and the final exam with mark 90 and weight 5 gives 450. The total weight is 10 and the total of mark times weight is 780, so the weighted mean is 78.
visual.caption: Weighted mean = total of (value × weight) ÷ total of the weights.

rows: Each value counts according to its weight
Always the same as the weighted mean when all weights are equal
Different when the weights are different

sections.heading: 4. Bar graphs and stacked bar graphs
sections.body_md: A **bar graph** shows the frequency of each category as the height of a bar; the bars have equal widths and gaps, and the scale starts at $0$. In a **stacked bar graph** each bar is divided into parts that add up to the total: the whole bar gives the **total** and each part gives one kind. Choose the graph by the question: separate categories, a bar graph; parts of totals, a stacked bar graph.

key_terms.definition_md: A graph of separate categories using bars of equal width with gaps.
A bar graph whose bars are cut into parts that add up to a total.

sections.heading: 5. Histograms and frequency polygons
sections.body_md: A **histogram** shows grouped data by bars with **no gaps**. With **equal widths** the height of a bar is the frequency. With **unequal widths** the height is the **frequency density** $= \dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$, so that the **area** of a bar is the frequency. A **frequency polygon** joins the points (class mark, frequency); an **empty class** is added at each end so that the polygon starts and ends on the axis.

key_terms.definition_md: A graph of grouped data with touching bars.
A line graph through the points (class mark, frequency).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Frequency tables (2–3 marks):* tally marks, frequencies that add up to the total.
- *Weighted mean (2–3 marks):* the products, their total, the total weight, the division.
- *Graphs (2–5 marks):* labelled axes, a scale, correct heights, no gaps in a histogram.

**Common mistakes**
1. Putting a value equal to an upper limit in that class.
2. Dividing by the number of values instead of the total weight.
3. Reading a part of a stacked bar as the total.
4. Using the frequency as the height for unequal class widths.
5. Leaving out the empty classes at the ends of a frequency polygon.

cards.front_md: What is primary data?
cards.back_md: Data collected by you, for your own purpose, by a survey, an interview, a measurement or an experiment.

cards.front_md: What is secondary data?
cards.back_md: Data collected earlier by someone else and taken from a source such as a report, a newspaper or a website.

cards.front_md: Which question should you ask before using data?
cards.back_md: Who collected it, and why?

cards.front_md: How are tally marks drawn?
cards.back_md: One stroke for each value; the fifth stroke goes across the four.

cards.front_md: What is the frequency of a value?
cards.back_md: The number of times it occurs.

cards.front_md: What do the frequencies add up to?
cards.back_md: The total number of observations.

cards.front_md: Why do we group data into classes?
cards.back_md: When there are many different values, a table with one row per value is too long.

cards.front_md: What is a class interval?
cards.back_md: A group of values from a lower limit to an upper limit, such as 30–45.

cards.front_md: Which class limit belongs to the class?
cards.back_md: The lower limit is included; the upper limit belongs to the next class.

cards.front_md: How do you find the class width?
cards.back_md: Upper limit minus lower limit.

cards.front_md: How do you find the class mark?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{\text{lower limit} + \text{upper limit}}{2}$, the mid-point of the class.

cards.front_md: What is a weight?
cards.back_md: A number that tells how much a value counts in an average.

cards.front_md: Formula for the weighted mean?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{x_1w_1 + x_2w_2 + \cdots}{w_1 + w_2 + \cdots}$.

cards.front_md: When is the weighted mean equal to the simple mean?
cards.back_md: When all the weights are equal.

cards.front_md: Which values are the weights in the average price of a mixture?
cards.back_md: The quantities of each variety.

cards.front_md: Which values are the weights in a cost-of-living figure?
cards.back_md: The share of each item in the budget.

cards.front_md: What do you divide by in a weighted mean?
cards.back_md: The total of the weights, not the number of values.

cards.front_md: What does a bar graph show?
cards.back_md: The frequency of each separate category, as the height of a bar.

cards.front_md: What must a bar graph scale start at?
cards.back_md: Zero.

cards.front_md: What is a stacked bar graph?
cards.back_md: A bar graph whose bars are cut into parts that add up to the total.

cards.front_md: In a stacked bar, what does the whole bar show, and each part?
cards.back_md: The whole bar shows the total; each part shows one kind.

cards.front_md: Which graph shows both totals and parts?
cards.back_md: A stacked bar graph.

cards.front_md: What is a histogram?
cards.back_md: A graph of grouped data with a bar for each class and no gaps.

cards.front_md: How does a histogram differ from a bar graph?
cards.back_md: A histogram has classes of numbers and no gaps; a bar graph has separate categories with gaps.

cards.front_md: What is the height of a bar in a histogram with equal widths?
cards.back_md: The frequency of the class.

cards.front_md: What is frequency density?
cards.back_md: $\dfrac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$.

cards.front_md: Why use frequency density for unequal widths?
cards.back_md: Then the area of a bar is the frequency, and the picture is fair.

cards.front_md: What is a frequency polygon?
cards.back_md: A line graph through the points (class mark, frequency).

cards.front_md: Why add an empty class at each end of a polygon?
cards.back_md: So that the polygon starts and ends on the axis.

cards.front_md: Through which points of a histogram does the polygon pass?
cards.back_md: The mid-points of the tops of the bars.

cards.front_md: Is the mean of ungrouped data part of this chapter?
cards.back_md: Only as the simple mean that we contrast with the weighted mean; mean, median and mode of data come later.

questions.stem_md: A frequency table groups the homework times of students into the classes $0$–$15$, $15$–$30$, $30$–$45$, $45$–$60$, $60$–$75$ and $75$–$90$ minutes. A student who worked exactly $30$ minutes is counted in the class
questions.solution_md: The lower limit of a class belongs to the class and the upper limit belongs to the next class. So $30$ goes into $30$–$45$, not into $15$–$30$.

questions.solution_md: Tea has $8$ students and lassi has $5$, so $8 + 5 = 13$ students. The value $19$ is tea plus milk, and $24$ is everybody except juice.

questions.stem_md: A shopkeeper in Surat mixes $20$ kg of dal at $\text{Rs } 90$ per kg with $30$ kg of dal at $\text{Rs } 80$ per kg. The average price of the mixture per kg is
questions.solution_md: The quantities are the weights: $\dfrac{20 \times 90 + 30 \times 80}{20 + 30} = \dfrac{1800 + 2400}{50} = \dfrac{4200}{50} = 84$. The value $85$ is the simple mean of $90$ and $80$, which ignores the quantities.

questions.stem_md: A student asks each of her classmates about the number of siblings and notes the answers herself. These data are called
questions.solution_md: Data collected directly by the investigator for her own purpose are primary data. Secondary data are taken from a source collected by someone else.

questions.stem_md: A team in Chennai writes a report using the rainfall figures of the last ten years published by the weather department. For the team these are
questions.solution_md: The team did not collect the figures itself; it took them from a published source. They are secondary data.

questions.stem_md: The class mark of the class $40$–$60$ is
questions.solution_md: The class mark is the mid-point of the class: $\dfrac{40 + 60}{2} = 50$. The value $20$ is the class width, and $100$ is the sum of the limits.

questions.stem_md: A table of the heights of students uses classes of width $5$ cm starting at $140$ cm. The fourth class is
questions.solution_md: The classes are $140$–$145$, $145$–$150$, $150$–$155$ and $155$–$160$. The fourth class is $155$–$160$, because its lower limit is $140 + 3 \times 5 = 155$.

questions.stem_md: In a histogram with equal class widths, the height of a bar is proportional to

options.text_md: the lower limit of the class

questions.solution_md: With equal widths the areas are in the same ratio as the heights, so the height shows the frequency of the class.

questions.stem_md: A school in Ranchi finds a term grade from three parts with weights $3$, $2$ and $5$. A student has $60$ in assignments, $80$ in the mid-term and $90$ in the final exam. The weighted mean is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{60 \times 3 + 80 \times 2 + 90 \times 5}{3 + 2 + 5} = \dfrac{180 + 160 + 450}{10} = \dfrac{790}{10} = 79$. The value $76.67$ is the simple mean, and $790$ forgets to divide by the total weight.

questions.stem_md: A tea seller in Darjeeling mixes $12$ kg of tea at $\text{Rs } 400$ per kg with $8$ kg of tea at $\text{Rs } 600$ per kg. The average price of the mixture per kg is
questions.solution_md: The quantities are the weights: $\dfrac{12 \times 400 + 8 \times 600}{12 + 8} = \dfrac{4800 + 4800}{20} = 480$. The value $500$ is the simple mean of the two prices, and $9600$ is the total cost.

questions.stem_md: The weighted mean of the numbers $40$ and $60$ is exactly their simple mean $50$ when

options.text_md: the two weights add up to $100$
both numbers have the same weight
the number $60$ has the larger weight
the number $40$ has the larger weight

questions.solution_md: If the weights are equal, $\dfrac{40w + 60w}{2w} = 50$. If $60$ has the larger weight the mean is above $50$, if $40$ has the larger weight it is below $50$, and weights such as $30$ and $70$ (which add up to $100$) give $54$.

questions.solution_md: The tally uses groups of five strokes, each with the fifth stroke across the four. $13 = 5 + 5 + 3$, so there are two crossed groups and three more strokes.

questions.stem_md: A principal wants to show, for each of four terms, how the students who passed are divided into grade A, grade B and grade C, and also how many passed in all. The best graph to draw is
questions.solution_md: A stacked bar graph shows the total by the height of the whole bar and the three grades by its parts. A simple bar graph shows one amount per bar, and a histogram or a frequency polygon is for grouped numbers.

questions.stem_md: Which of these graphs has no gaps between its bars?
questions.solution_md: The classes of a histogram follow each other without a break, so its bars touch. The bars of a bar graph and of a stacked bar graph have gaps.

**Reason (R):** In a weighted mean, a value with a larger weight counts more than a value with a smaller weight.

Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md: Why must the heights of the bars be frequency densities, and not frequencies, in a histogram with unequal class widths?

answer.model_answer_md:
If the heights were the frequencies, a wide class would have a tall-looking bar and would seem more important than it is. For example, a class of width $40$ with frequency $8$ would be drawn about as high as a class of width $10$ with frequency $8$, but it is spread over four times the range.

With height $=$ frequency $\div$ class width, the area of every bar $=$ the frequency, so the picture is fair.

questions.solution_md: Area of a bar must stand for the frequency.

questions.stem_md: In a school in Pune the final score is made from homework (weight $10$), class tests (weight $20$), project (weight $30$) and the final exam (weight $40$). Aman has $90$, $70$, $80$ and $60$ in them. Bela has $60$, $75$, $70$ and $80$. (a) Find Aman's weighted score. (b) Find the simple mean of Aman's four marks. (c) Find Bela's weighted score. (d) Who ranks higher by the weighted score? (e) What mark in the final exam would give Bela a weighted score of exactly $80$, with her other marks the same?

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $\dfrac{90 \times 10 + 70 \times 20 + 80 \times 30 + 60 \times 40}{100} = \dfrac{900 + 1400 + 2400 + 2400}{100} = \dfrac{7100}{100} = 71$.

**(b)** Simple mean $= \dfrac{90 + 70 + 80 + 60}{4} = 75$.

**(c)** $\dfrac{60 \times 10 + 75 \times 20 + 70 \times 30 + 80 \times 40}{100} = \dfrac{600 + 1500 + 2100 + 3200}{100} = \dfrac{7400}{100} = 74$.

**(d)** Bela ($74 > 71$), although Aman has the higher simple mean ($75$ against $71.25$): the final exam has the largest weight.

**(e)** Bela needs $80 \times 100 = 8000$ in total. Her other marks give $600 + 1500 + 2100 = 4200$, so $40x = 3800$ and $x = 95$.

questions.solution_md: Weighted means with the weights as percentages; then the unknown mark.

questions.stem_md: A trader in Jaipur mixes three varieties of tea: $20$ kg at $\text{Rs } 250$ per kg, $30$ kg at $\text{Rs } 300$ per kg and $50$ kg at $\text{Rs } 360$ per kg. (a) Find the total cost of the three varieties. (b) Find the total quantity. (c) Find the average cost of the mixture per kg. (d) Find the simple mean of the three prices. (e) At what price per kg must the mixture be sold to make a profit of $15\%$ on the average cost?

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** $20 \times 250 + 30 \times 300 + 50 \times 360 = 5000 + 9000 + 18000 = \text{Rs } 32000$.

**(b)** $20 + 30 + 50 = 100$ kg.

**(c)** Average cost $= \dfrac{32000}{100} = \text{Rs } 320$ per kg (a weighted mean, with the quantities as weights).

**(d)** Simple mean $= \dfrac{250 + 300 + 360}{3} \approx 303.33$, which is lower because it ignores that the dearest tea has the largest quantity.

**(e)** Selling price $= 320 \times 1.15 = \text{Rs } 368$ per kg.

questions.solution_md: Total cost, total quantity, weighted mean, simple mean, profit of 15 percent.

questions.passage_md: A fair in Pushkar keeps a record of the minutes spent by $120$ visitors at a craft stall. The times are grouped in the classes $0$–$10$, $10$–$20$, $20$–$40$ and $40$–$60$ minutes, with frequencies $30$, $36$, $36$ and $18$. The histogram is drawn with the frequency density as the height.

children.stem_md: The heights of the bars are frequency densities, and not frequencies, because

options.text_md: the class widths are not all equal

children.solution_md: The classes have widths $10$, $10$, $20$ and $20$. With unequal widths the area of a bar, and not its height, must show the frequency, so the height is the frequency divided by the class width.

children.stem_md: Find the frequency density of the class $20$–$40$.
**(i)** Find the area of the bar for the class $40$–$60$ and say what it shows.

answer.model_answer_md: The height is $\dfrac{18}{20} = 0.9$ and the width is $20$, so the area is $0.9 \times 20 = 18$. It equals the frequency of the class.

children.solution_md: Area of a bar = height times width = frequency.

marking_scheme.step: It is the frequency of the class

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** How many visitors spent $20$ minutes or more at the stall?

answer.model_answer_md: The classes $20$–$40$ and $40$–$60$ have frequencies $36$ and $18$, so $36 + 18 = 54$ visitors.

alternatives.solution_md: Add the frequencies of the last two classes.

options.text_md: across the four strokes before it
as a separate stroke after a gap

questions.solution_md: The fifth stroke goes across the four strokes before it, so that the strokes come in groups of five that are easy to count.

questions.stem_md: The frequencies in a frequency table add up to
questions.solution_md: Every observation is counted once, so the frequencies add up to the number of observations. For the shoe sizes of $30$ students they add up to $3 + 7 + 11 + 6 + 3 = 30$.

questions.stem_md: The weighted mean of the values $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$ with weights $w_1$, $w_2$, $w_3$ is
questions.solution_md: Multiply each value by its weight, add, and divide by the total of the weights. The second expression is the simple mean, and the third forgets to divide by the total weight.

questions.stem_md: The scale on the vertical axis of a bar graph should start at

options.text_md: the smallest value in the data
the largest value in the data

questions.solution_md: Heights of bars are compared by eye, so they must be in the same ratio as the values. For the values $20$, $40$, $60$ the heights are in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$ from $0$, but a scale starting at $10$ gives $10 : 30 : 50$, which is not the same.

questions.stem_md: The bars of a bar graph can be put in any order without changing what the graph shows, but the bars of a histogram cannot be rearranged.
questions.solution_md: The bars of a bar graph stand for separate categories, so their order does not matter. The bars of a histogram stand for classes of numbers that follow one another, so they must stay in the order of the classes. The statement is true.

questions.stem_md: The sum of all the frequencies of a frequency table is the total number of ____.
questions.solution_md: Each observation is counted once in the table, so the frequencies add up to the total number of observations. So the blank is observations.

questions.stem_md: A teacher says: "When the papers have different importance, the weighted mean of a student's marks is fairer than the simple mean." Explain this with an example of two marks, $50$ and $90$, where the second paper has $3$ times the weight of the first.

answer.model_answer_md:
In a weighted mean a paper that counts more has more effect on the result.

Weighted mean $= \dfrac{50 \times 1 + 90 \times 3}{1 + 3} = \dfrac{320}{4} = 80$, while the simple mean is $\dfrac{50 + 90}{2} = 70$.

The simple mean ignores the fact that the second paper counts three times as much, so the weighted mean $80$ is fairer.

questions.solution_md: Weighted mean 80 against simple mean 70, with the reason.

marking_scheme.step: The paper with more weight should count more
